entries.surface: **A bundle attributes to a BUILD, and it can only name one if the host gives it one (G3, opened 2026-08-18).** `host` carries `name` + `version` and MAY carry `commit` / `build`, all self-reported. **A commit does not determine the artifact that ran.** A tier-2 host measured this directly: the *same commit* (`21db7e21d`), rebuilt hours later into a new image with identical revision…
entries.note: configuration, scored **283 pass / 22 fail** against **303 / 2** for the first build — because its container build ran `npm install` rather than `npm ci`, so two builds resolved different transitive dependency versions. Nothing in the bundle could distinguish the two runs: same `suite.version`, same `host.name`/`version`, same `discovery.sha256`, same `targetConfigurationSha256` — that hash covers the *advertised configuration*, not the dependency closure that executed. — Consequences, stated rather than left to inference: — - A bundle is evidence about **one execution of one build**. It is not evidence about a commit, and re-running "the same commit" is not a re-check unless the build is deterministic. — - A host SHOULD populate `host.build` with an identifier that names **what actually executed**, and SHOULD make its builds reproducible (a lockfile-respecting install: `npm ci`, not `npm install`) so that identifier means something. — **Which identifier depends on when the bundle is produced, and the strongest one is not always reachable** *(amended 2026-08-18 after a tier-1 host pointed out the ordering constraint)*. A bundle baked **into** the image at certify time — vendored so it is servable without a runtime recompute, which is what makes it tamper-evident — is written when no image and therefore no digest yet exists. Telling such a host to record an image digest would force it either to certify post-deploy, losing the baking property, or to ship a second revision purely to stamp one. Neither is intended. In rough order of strength, and each is only as good as what it pins: — | Identifier | Available | Pins | — | --- | --- | --- | — | container image digest | after the build | the exact artifact — strongest, but not at bake time | — | builder-assigned build id | during the build | that build, if the builder's ids are unique and retained | — | digest of the **resolved dependency manifest** (e.g. the lockfile, or the resolved tree) | at certify time | the dependency closure — the thing that actually varied in the measurement above | — The last row deserves emphasis, because it is available exactly when a baked bundle is written **and** it addresses the observed failure directly: what differed between the two builds of one commit was the resolved closure, not the image identity per se. A host whose install respects its lockfile has `commit` + lockfile digest jointly determining the closure; a host whose install does not has neither pinning anything, which is the defect. Recording *which* kind of identifier `host.build` holds is more useful than recording the strongest-sounding one. — - **First bundle measured against a reproducibly built image (recorded 2026-08-19).** The same tier-2 host that measured the divergence above made its builds lockfile-respecting and published bundle v2 #15 against the result (`workflow-runtime-00572-noc`, suite `1.136.11`). Two things about the path there are worth recording, because "just use `npm ci`" understates it: the switch **failed the build loudly**, naming five packages missing from the lockfile, and a follow-up attempt to filter them out with `--omit=optional` also failed — the installer validates lock/manifest sync *before* honoring omit filters, so that flag can never reach the problem. What worked was pinning the installer to the version that **wrote** the lock. The seam is writer/reader agreement, not the lockfile alone. The host's own stated residual is that the lockfile is still missing entries an older installer expects and was pinned around rather than regenerated, and that its guard test can assert a pin exists but not that the pin is the right one — so this is a build that is now *re-checkable*, not one that is proven closed. — - A verifier re-checking a claim MUST re-run against the **same build**, not merely the same commit, or say which it did. — This is a host-build property, so the spec **requires** nothing here beyond honest reporting; it is recorded because a bundle that cannot name its own build inputs is weaker evidence than its shape suggests, and the format previously implied otherwise. Same family as the dispositions RFC 0148 §A introduced: the artifact must not read as attesting more than it observed.

entries.surface: **A file-level disposition can certify a requirement the run never exercised (G8, opened 2026-08-19).** A scenario file records `executed-pass` when it ran with at least one passing assertion and no failures — the RFC 0148 §C vacuity rule, which catches a file that asserted *nothing*. It cannot distinguish a file that asserted **the requirement** from one that asserted only a **positive…
entries.note: control** or a setup precondition before soft-skipping the requirement-bearing leg. — **The mechanism is precise and was measured, not inferred** (reported by a tier-1 host calling `resolveFileRecord` directly, no host involved). The file's noted reason is honoured in exactly two branches: when `assertionCount === 0`, and when *every* test called `ctx.skip()`. A `return softSkip(...)` produces a **pass** state, not a skip — so in a file that asserts anything at all and then soft-skips, **neither branch fires, the note is silently discarded, and the row reads `executed-pass`.** `['pass'], assertionCount 1, noted blocked` resolves to `executed-pass` with the reason dropped. — This is the same defect as the one already recorded in that function's own comment — notes written *after* `ctx.skip()` threw, which left seven files carrying notes the ledger never saw. **Note-after-skip was fixed; note-after-assertion was not**, and it hid for the same reason: nothing goes red. — The perverse property is worth stating plainly: **the better the scenario, the more convincingly it mis-certifies.** A positive control is exactly what makes a negative assertion trustworthy, and it is also what supplies the assertion that suppresses the note. A thin scenario with no control trips the vacuity rule and is caught. — Scope, stated as what it is: **36 scenario files carry 75 `softSkip` calls positioned after their first assertion.** That is a count of *positions*, not of wrong rows — the note is only dropped on a run that takes that path, so on a fully-capable host most never fire. **It bites on partially-capable hosts**, which is precisely the population a matrix exists to describe and the one where `blocked` / `inapplicable` / `executed-pass` carries all the meaning. A confirmed instance: `feedback-fork-not-copied.test.ts` asserts a `201` setup precondition and then returns `softSkip('inapplicable', 'fork unsupported')`, so a fork-less host records `executed-pass` for *"a fork of an annotated run starts with zero annotations"* — a requirement it cannot attempt. — **This is not an RFC 0148 §A violation on §A's own terms** — §A names "a plain test return, caught exception converted to a return, or empty assertion body", and this case has a non-empty assertion body. It is the harm §A exists to prevent, at a granularity §A's zero-assertion test cannot see. — **Durable fix (2026-09-02, suite 1.153.0): per-`it` rows.** Every test now records its own ledger row (`openwop.it.<file>.<title-slug>`, `conformance/requirements.json`), so the requirement's own row carries the soft-skip disposition while the positive control's row carries the pass. The file-level row and its `partial-witness:` marker remain for readers of older bundles. — **Interim (2026-08-19): the note is no longer discarded.** When a file resolves to `executed-pass` and a note exists, the note is retained as `detail` behind a `partial-witness:` marker. This changes no disposition — a conservative choice, because honouring the note unconditionally would downgrade a file that legitimately completed its requirement *and* soft-skipped an optional extra leg, trading a false positive for a false negative. Affected rows are now self-identifying in every bundle (`executed-pass` with a `partial-witness:` detail), which turns a static count of positions into a measured count of real occurrences. The durable fix is per-`it` recording rather than per-file, and it should follow that evidence rather than precede it.

entries.surface: Portable per-run parameter deferral
entries.note: Some hosts (e.g., openwop-app, ADR 0237) want chain parameters to stay overridable per-run rather than frozen at drop time. Expansion-time substitution (this spec) forbids leaving `{{params.*}}` tokens in the persisted definition because they are not a spec'd runtime construct and break cross-host portability. A **portable** deferral mode would have expansion materialize the chain's `parameters` into top-level workflow `variables[]` and rewrite `{{params.x}}` into a spec'd runtime binding (for prompt-bearing config, the PromptTemplate `{{varName}}` with `source: "variable"` per `prompts.md` §"Variable interpolation"), gated behind a new capability with replay/event-log determinism for the run-scoped variable bag. **Recommended: a follow-up additive RFC**, not a relaxation of the expansion-time MUST.

Host-side lifecycle, not a wire-shape concern; tracked in [`docs/KNOWN-LIMITS.md`](../../docs/KNOWN-LIMITS.md).
